title: How To Begin 2015 On The Right Classroom Management Foot management-foot/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin lays out a plan for making the most of the fresh-start opportunity that returning from an extended break offers, since students typically come back more relaxed, open, and receptive—an advantage that fades quickly if not seized immediately. His five recommended steps are: personally greeting each student at the door to build rapport, modeling and practicing the first classroom routine as if for the first time, spending unscripted time enjoying and reconnecting with students, thoroughly reteaching the classroom management plan with no exceptions, and establishing a calm, unhurried pace for the rest of the day. Linsin argues that only a class that had completely fallen apart before break needs a full first-day-of-school reset; for most classrooms, a detailed review paired with genuine commitment to consistent principles is sufficient to capitalize on students' renewed receptiveness.
points: Students returning from an extended break tend to be more relaxed, open, and receptive—an advantage that fades quickly unless teachers act immediately.
Step 1: personally greet each student at the door to build instant rapport before the day begins.
Step 2: model and practice the very first classroom routine of the day as though teaching it for the first time.
Step 3: spend unscripted time reconnecting with students and sharing holiday experiences to strengthen rapport.
Steps 4-5: thoroughly reteach the classroom management plan with no exceptions, and establish a calm, unhurried pace for the rest of the day.
quotes: Students return from extended breaks more open, more relaxed, and more appreciative of school.
So you must strike while the iron is hot. You must strike the moment they arrive at your door.

These fleeting moments cost nothing, but mean so much. They build instant rapport and likability and launch a chain of reciprocal kindness and thoughtfulness that will spread throughout your classroom.

By reviewing and perfecting a common routine first thing in the morning, you’ll be sending a message of excellence that will transfer to everything they do—behavior, work habits, attentiveness, and so much more.
Teachers who struggle with classroom management tend to do everything too fast and with an undercurrent of tension, which causes excitability, distraction, and misbehavior.
Unless your class had completely fallen off the rails before vacation, there is little reason to approach the first day back as if it’s the first day of school.
